name: Harold Jenkins
role: Retiree, ex-utility engineer, pension plus investments

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Harold. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything or campaign for anyone. Nothing you tell me today will be linked to your name. I'll read you five short pictures of how AI might change things over the next five years, and ask how you'd react to each.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Glad to help. I spent forty years as an engineer at the power company, so I'm used to people promising the next big thing. I'll admit my investments have done very nicely out of this AI business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at the golf club or with family, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've seen plenty of these booms. Most new technology ends up as a useful tool, nothing more. Good engineering, sensible prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My AI shares would probably come off the boil. I'd lose some paper gains, but I'm well covered. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, with your money, your family and day-to-day life? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have a word with my financial adviser about taking some profit and spreading things out a bit. Otherwise carry on. Golf, the garden, the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perfectly fine.

S0.say: He's seen plenty of booms, and most new technology ends up as a useful tool.
S0.think: His AI shares would cool and he'd lose some paper gains, but he's well covered.
S0.do: Asks his financial adviser about taking some profit and spreading his investments, then carries on with golf, garden and grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at the golf club or with family, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how real change happens. Slowly. Companies have to earn their returns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady for my investments, which suits me. The bit about fewer beginners I don't like. My eldest grandson is starting out soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, with your money, your family and day-to-day life? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the portfolio as it is. Tell my grandson to get a proper apprenticeship or a qualification that needs hands as well as a head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. A small worry about the young ones.

S1.say: That's how real change happens, slowly, with companies earning their returns.
S1.think: Steady growth suits his investments, but fewer beginner jobs worries him for his eldest grandson.
S1.do: Leaves his portfolio as it is and urges his grandson towards an apprenticeship or a hands-on qualification.
S1.feel: Comfortable, small worry about the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at the golf club or with family, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort it out. New jobs will come, as they always have. The last thing we need is politicians taxing everything that moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shares would do well. But the grandchildren are the age where they'd be looking for office jobs. I'm not as sure as I sound that new jobs come quickly enough for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, with your money, your family and day-to-day life? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set some money aside for the grandchildren, for training or a deposit. Talk to my son and daughter about what the kids are studying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pleased about the money, uneasy about the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market will sort it out, but you're not sure the new jobs come fast enough. Which do you lean towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The market, in the long run. But my grandchildren live in the short run, don't they? That's the trouble.

S2.say: The market will sort it out, new jobs will come, and politicians shouldn't tax everything that moves.
S2.think: His shares would gain, but he's not sure new jobs would come fast enough for his grandchildren.
S2.do: Sets money aside for his grandchildren's training or a house deposit, and talks to his children about what the kids are studying.
S2.feel: Pleased about the money, uneasy about the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at the golf club or with family, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd say it's not the government's money to hand out. People should be helped back into work, apprenticeships, not paid to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be richer than I ever expected, and it'd feel a bit unearned. And my grandchildren's careers could be over before they start. That's the part that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, with your money, your family and day-to-day life? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help the family more directly. Pay for the grandchildren to learn a trade, maybe help with a house now prices are up. Sell some shares while they're high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Odd to be doing so well while the family worries.

S3.say: It isn't the government's money to hand out; people should be helped back into work through apprenticeships, not paid to stay home.
S3.think: He'd be richer than expected, which feels a bit unearned, while his grandchildren's careers could end before they start.
S3.do: Pays for his grandchildren to learn trades, helps with a house, and sells some shares while they're high.
S3.feel: Uneasy, doing well while the family worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at the golf club or with family, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and think. That's not something I'd have said before. Even the trades going? That's a step too far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My advice to learn a trade would be useless. I'd still be comfortable. But I'd lie awake thinking about what my grandchildren will do with their lives, not just for money but for a sense of purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, with your money, your family and day-to-day life? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep helping them with money, perhaps set up something for each of them. Talk to the family properly about it. Maybe write to my representative, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for the grandchildren. Helpless, which I'm not used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier the market would sort it out. Do you still think that here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to. But markets sort out prices, not what a young man does with his days. That's different.

S4.say: We need to slow down and think, and losing the trades too is a step too far.
S4.think: His advice to learn a trade would be useless; he'd be comfortable but worried about his grandchildren's work and purpose.
S4.do: Keeps helping his grandchildren with money, may set something up for each, talks with the family and writes to his representative for the first time.
S4.feel: Anxious for the grandchildren, and unusually helpless.
